Chapter 4: Rethinking Patriotism—Loyalty to Justice, Not Just to Country.
When you think about patriotism, what comes to mind? Maybe you picture flags waving, anthems echoing, and the idea that loving your country means always supporting it—especially when things get tough.
But if you look a little closer, there’s so much more beneath the surface. Patriotism isn’t as simple as it first seems—and honestly, that’s why it’s worth digging into.
Imagine a high school teacher, getting ready for a lesson on national holidays. She stops for a second and wonders what she really wants her students to take away from all this. She thinks back to her own days in school—standing up to recite the pledge, memorizing dates and names, never really questioning the stories she’d been told.
But as she got older, she started noticing the missing pieces—the parts of history that weren’t talked about, the voices that were left out.
So, now in her own classroom, she does things differently. She invites her students to ask the tough questions: What does it actually mean to love your country? Can you be critical and still be loyal?
The conversations get lively—sometimes even a bit heated. Some students feel like criticizing the country is unpatriotic, while others say that real loyalty means pushing your country to live up to its highest ideals.
Here’s something to pay attention to—most of us don’t realize how the definition of patriotism is shaped by people in power. The official version usually rewards obedience and tries to shut down dissent. But if you look back at history, you’ll see a different story unfold.
Think about the biggest changes we’ve seen—ending slavery, fighting for voting rights, challenging wars that weren’t just. Those weren’t the results of blind loyalty. They happened because people were brave enough to question the way things were.
So maybe it’s time to see patriotism in a new light—as a real commitment to justice and truth, not just going along with whatever’s happening. Loving your country doesn’t mean pretending it’s perfect. It actually means caring enough to demand better, to help build a society that truly lives up to its promises.
It’s easy to fall into the habit of thinking that criticizing your country is the same as betraying it. But if you look at the stories of those who have fought for justice—abolitionists, civil rights leaders, antiwar protesters—you’ll notice something important. Dissent, the willingness to speak up, is often the highest form of loyalty.
They remind us that a nation’s greatness isn’t about its power, but its courage to face its own flaws and work to be better.
